extracted.intended_audience: educated general readers of The Spectator; poets, literary critics, and public commentators
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and exemplars for composing short commemorative pieces (epigrams/epitaphs) and for offering praise—covering tone, specificity, and rhetorical devices—as well as several related practical/projectual notices (club selection, product subscription terms).

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection of club representatives by merit
rubrics_metrics.description: Issue writs to established clubs requiring them 'to chuse out of their respective Bodies a Person of the greatest Merit, and to return his name' before a set day for assembly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The organiser expects the chosen persons to make the presiding club 'the very Flower and Quintescence of all other Clubs.' (Context: a proposal for forming a club by calling the best members from other clubs.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Epitaph/praise should not depend on fable
rubrics_metrics.description: Our Praise is trifling when it depends upon Fable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When praise rests on a mythical or false premise it is trivial; authors should avoid making encomia that hinge on accepted but fictive stories (example: Orpheus fable makes the epigram pious in its original age but less esteemed by later knowledge).

rubrics_metrics.name: Epitaph/praise must avoid wrong qualifications
rubrics_metrics.description: Praise is false when it depends upon wrong qualifications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not attribute qualities that are untrue of the subject; misqualification renders praise dishonest rather than laudatory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid general praise; prefer circumscribed particulars
rubrics_metrics.description: General praise is meaningless and better joined with something that 'circumscribes and bounds it to the Qualities of our Subject.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A panegyric that is too broad may belong to any great person; tie praise to particular, distinguishing attributes of the subject (example critique of the Euripides epigram which lacks particulars).

rubrics_metrics.name: Match the tone and humour of the subject when praising
rubrics_metrics.description: When praising, enter into the spirit of the subject so that the humour and images resemble those of the person praised (e.g., the Anacreon epigram's easy, gay humour mirrors its subject).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt imagery, mood, and diction appropriate to the subject's known style; this creates a congruent and fitting compliment rather than an external or misplaced admiration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fix praise only where there is a real foundation in merit
rubrics_metrics.description: When they would praise, they cautiously avoid every looser Qualification, and fix only where there is a real Foundation in Merit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Praise should be anchored in actual, demonstrable accomplishments; avoid flattering by vague or overstated claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of irony as a refined mode of praise
rubrics_metrics.description: An Irony is look'd upon as the finest Palliative of Praise; and very often conveys the noblest Panegyrick under the Appearance of Satire.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deploy subtle irony to convey high compliment under the guise of mock-accusation or satire (example: the epigram that pretends to accuse Homer of plagiarism is in fact a supreme compliment).

rubrics_metrics.name: Epitaphic praise should reflect subject's particular excellence and relation to place
rubrics_metrics.description: Good epigrams situate the poet's work and character (e.g., Menander's purity of language is linked to Athens, 'you make your Athens shine').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tie a subject's virtues to concrete accomplishments or civic/national associations to make praise feel rooted and explanatory rather than empty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epitaph style: grave philosophic humour for leaving the public with grace
rubrics_metrics.description: An epitaph may use 'grave and philosophick Humour' to speak of oneself as withdrawn from the world, serving as an instruction on how to 'leave the Publick with a good Grace' (example: Cowley's epitaph).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A composed, mildly humorous self-portrait in an epitaph can instruct and charm; prefer contemplative wit over vain boasting in memorial pieces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use decent and proper English in legal/public speech; avoid cant
rubrics_metrics.description: Lawyers should 'let their Clients have a little decent and proper English ...' and 'leave off such low and unnatural Expressions' (criticising terms like 'stripp'd', 'saddled', 'hung up').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public and formal discourse (especially in courts) should avoid coarse, cant, or vulgar expressions and prefer clear, proper English; the complaint notes that clients paying for counsel deserve decorous language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Celestial globe accuracy standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Place fixed stars according to true longitude and latitude from correct observations (Hevelius, Cassini, Flamsteed, Halley); draw constellations 'in a curious, new, and particular manner'; represent each star's true magnitude and delineate tracks of observed comets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Globes should be made 'more exact, instructive, and useful' by using the best available astronomical observations so that magnitudes and positions are discernible at inspection; this is advanced as a selling point to subscribers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Terrestrial globe accuracy and content requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Redraw Asia, Africa, and America in a wholly new manner correcting latitudes/longitudes (some altered by up to 10–20 degrees), insert omitted countries/cities/rivers/lakes from late navigators' discoveries, and visibly express the course of trade-winds and monsoons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize and correct prior errors in major globes; include newly discovered geographic detail and wind patterns to make the globe useful for navigation and study.

rubrics_metrics.name: Globe subscription and delivery terms (price, payment, exclusivity, refund, ordering)
rubrics_metrics.description: Subscribers to a pair of 30-inch celestial and terrestrial globes pay 25 pounds (10 pounds down, 15 on delivery); each subscriber will receive a pair adorned and supposedly worth more than the asking price; subscribers' arms/names may be inserted; delivery within 12 months after 30 subscribers are completed; pairs not sold later under 30 pounds; money refunded if 30 subscribers not obtained within four months via appointed agent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These contractual conditions set expectations for price, payment schedule, personalization, delivery lead-time contingent on a minimum number, resale restrictions, and a refund mechanism—useful both as consumer protections and marketing terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art and public works should be put to noble, useful ends
rubrics_metrics.description: An organ erected in St. Paul's should be of such art and magnificence as to transcend previous works and 'apply the Power of Sounds' to strike minds in a place of worship, producing forgetfulness of care and hope of rapture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public expenditure on arts (here, organ building) is defended as a worthy alternative to wasteful opera spending—art should serve the public good and inspire religious/national sentiment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualities that mark a great/complete genius
rubrics_metrics.description: Great minds (Bacon, Boyle, Leonardo) display extraordinary force of nature, compass of thought, indefatigable study, ability to sketch new tracks of enquiry, perform numerous experiments, mastery across multiple arts and sciences, bodily and moral virtues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples suggest that greatness combines breadth of knowledge, industriousness, original contribution (outlining new questions), technical skill across disciplines, and decent moral character; these are held up as models for admiration and emulation.
